title: The PRD Nobody Read
body: You spent three days writing a 14-page PRD. It has user stories, acceptance criteria, edge cases, a competitive analysis. You posted it in Slack. Two emoji reactions. One is a 👀 from an intern. The other is a 🎉 from a bot. You check the Notion analytics. Four views. One is you. Three are the bot indexing the page.

choices.title: Rewrite it as a one-pager with bullets
choices.body: Distill 14 pages into one. Admit that brevity was the ask all along.

choices.title: Ask Claude to summarize it for you
choices.body: Paste 14 pages into a prompt. Get back 3 sentences that are better than your intro.

choices.title: Walk desk-to-desk and force people to read it
choices.body: Become the human push notification. They'll remember you. Not fondly.

title: The Standup About Standups
body: Your team's standup is 28 minutes. It was supposed to be 15. Someone suggests a retro on the standup format. Someone else suggests a standup for the retro. You open your mouth to say 'let's take this offline' and realize you have become the meeting.

choices.title: Kill the standup, move to async updates
choices.body: Replace the meeting with a Slack bot. Save 140 minutes a week. Feel existentially redundant.

choices.title: Enforce a strict 15-minute timebox
choices.body: Become the clock cop. Everyone respects the time. Nobody respects you.

choices.title: Let it sprawl, at least people are talking
choices.body: Meetings are your natural habitat. If they shrink, so do you.

title: Jira Ticket Archaeology
body: You're grooming the backlog and find a ticket from 2021 labeled 'P1 - URGENT.' It has 47 comments, three reassignments, and no resolution. The original reporter left the company. The feature it describes shipped six months ago under a different name. Nobody closed the ticket. The ticket is you.

choices.title: Close it with a smug comment
choices.body: 'Resolved: shipped as part of Project Phoenix, Q3 2024.' Add a party emoji. Feel nothing.

choices.title: Use it as ammo for backlog bankruptcy
choices.body: Declare the backlog dead. Start fresh. 200 tickets move to a graveyard board named 'Someday.'

choices.title: Add another comment and reassign it
choices.body: The cycle continues. You are now part of the problem. The ticket outlives us all.

title: "What Do You Actually Produce?"
body: All-hands Q&A. The CEO takes a question from an engineer: 'What does the product team actually produce?' The CEO pauses. Looks at you. Says: 'Great question.' The silence that follows has a texture. You can feel your role dissolving in real-time like a sugar cube in coffee nobody ordered.

choices.title: Give a polished answer about alignment and velocity
choices.body: You say words like 'cross-functional leverage' and 'outcome orientation.' Nobody is convinced. Including you.

choices.title: Show the roadmap receipts
choices.body: Pull up metrics. Show shipped features, revenue impact, velocity gains. Fight with data.

choices.title: Laugh it off and die inside
choices.body: You make a joke. Everyone laughs. You go home and update your resume.

title: The Notion Empire
body: Your Notion workspace has 847 pages. Templates for templates. Databases linked to databases. A wiki nobody reads, a roadmap nobody follows, and a meeting notes archive that constitutes a legal record of indecision. It is a monument. It is your monument.

choices.title: Show it off in a blog post
choices.body: Turn organizational theater into content. Your Notion setup gets 200 likes on Twitter.

choices.title: Realize nobody uses it and feel devastated
choices.body: You check page analytics. The most-viewed page is 'Team Lunch Preferences.' Your PRD template has 3 views.

choices.title: Burn it down, start with AI
choices.body: Delete 800 pages. Replace with an AI-generated knowledge base. It's worse but cheaper.

title: Engineers Are Talking to Claude Directly
body: You overhear two engineers in the kitchen. 'I just ask Claude what to build next.' 'Yeah, it writes better user stories than the PRDs.' They see you. One says 'oh hey, we should loop you in on that.' You were the loop. The loop doesn't need a loop anymore.

choices.title: Ask to see their Claude prompts
choices.body: If the machine is doing your job, at least learn how it's doing it.

choices.title: Reassert yourself as the decision-maker
choices.body: Schedule a meeting about 'product process alignment.' Defend the org chart with your body.

choices.title: Join them and co-pilot the prompts
choices.body: If you can't beat the workflow, embed yourself in it. Become the human in the loop.

title: Roadmap Theater
body: Board meeting tomorrow. Your VP wants 'the roadmap.' You have a roadmap. It's a fiction you update quarterly that everyone treats as scripture until they ignore it. You color-code things that haven't been scoped and put dates on work nobody's committed to. The board loves it.

choices.title: Make it beautiful and vague
choices.body: Timelines say 'H1' instead of dates. Everything is 'on track' because nothing has a track.

choices.title: Be honest about uncertainty
choices.body: Add confidence intervals. Say 'we don't know' in a slide. Your VP's eye twitches.

choices.title: Let AI generate three roadmap versions
choices.body: Optimistic, realistic, pessimistic. Show all three. The board picks optimistic. You knew they would.

title: The Retro Where Nothing Changes
body: Sprint retro. Post-its on a virtual board. 'What went well: we shipped.' 'What didn't: scope creep.' 'Action items: be more disciplined about scope.' This is the same retro you ran last sprint. And the sprint before that. The post-its are a prayer wheel that never reaches god.

choices.title: Actually enforce the action items this time
choices.body: Create Jira tickets for the action items. They will join the other 200 unresolved action items.

choices.title: Cancel retros, go async instead
choices.body: Kill the ceremony. Save the time. Lose the one meeting where people are honest.

choices.title: Do a feelings check instead
choices.body: Ask people how they're actually doing. The room gets quiet. Then someone cries. Progress?

title: OKR Season
body: It's OKR season. You've written 'Increase user activation by 15%' for the third consecutive quarter. Nobody knows what activation means. You defined it differently each time. The key result is measured by a dashboard that's been broken since August. The O is aspirational. The KRs are fictional. This is corporate astrology.

choices.title: Write OKRs you actually believe in
choices.body: Set modest, real goals. Your VP says they're 'not ambitious enough.' Ambitious means impossible.

choices.title: Copy last quarter's with bigger numbers
choices.body: 15% becomes 25%. Nobody will check. Nobody checked last time.

choices.title: Propose killing OKRs entirely
choices.body: Suggest 'outcomes over frameworks.' Your VP looks at you like you suggested arson.

title: Stakeholder Management (Babysitting)
body: Three VPs want different features. Sales wants a dashboard. Marketing wants an integration. Engineering wants to refactor. You are in a room mediating between adults who make more money than you about things they understand less than you. This is your job. Your entire job.

choices.title: Build a prioritization framework and force a decision
choices.body: RICE scores, impact mapping, the whole show. They ignore the framework and pick the loudest VP's feature.

choices.title: Say yes to everything and quietly descope later
choices.body: Agree in the room. Cut in the sprint. The ancient PM art of strategic ambiguity.

choices.title: Escalate and make it their problem
choices.body: Pass the hot potato up. Your VP loves 'empowering you to own decisions' until there's an actual decision.

title: AI Writes Better User Stories Than You
body: You paste a feature description into Claude. It generates acceptance criteria, edge cases, and test scenarios in 30 seconds. The output is better than what you wrote last week. Cleaner. More thorough. You spent four hours on yours. The machine spent tokens. You are an expensive token.

choices.title: Use it as a first draft
choices.body: Let the machine write structure. Add the taste. Hope taste is worth $130K/year.

choices.title: Hide the output and keep writing stories manually
choices.body: Pretend you didn't see it. Guard the craft. The craft may not be worth guarding.

choices.title: Show the team and suggest everyone use it
choices.body: Democratize the tool. Now everyone can write user stories. Now nobody needs you to.

title: The Art of Professional Vagueness
body: You're on a call with a client. They ask when a feature ships. You say 'we're targeting Q2.' They ask which Q2. You say 'this year's.' They ask for a date. You say 'we're working through the details.' You've said nothing three times and they're satisfied. This is your superpower. It might also be your entire skill.

choices.title: Get specific and commit to a date
choices.body: Give a real date. Miss it by two weeks. Learn that honesty is punished.

choices.title: Stay vague and manage expectations like a diplomat
choices.body: You are a professional ambiguity engine. The role exists because specificity is dangerous.

choices.title: Build a self-serve status page
choices.body: Automate the vagueness. The status page says 'In Progress' for everything. It's accurate.

title: The Title Grab
body: LinkedIn is full of people adding 'AI' to their title. 'Head of AI Product.' 'VP of AI Strategy.' 'Chief AI Product Officer.' You have the same PM job you had last year. But the URL in your Notion workspace still says 'AI_Roadmap_v2.' That's close enough, right?

choices.title: Update your title to 'AI Product Lead'
choices.body: Nobody approves this. You just change your LinkedIn. Your manager finds out in a week.

choices.title: Propose a real AI product role to leadership
choices.body: Write a job description. Pitch the need. It's you pitching that you should exist, but with AI in front.

choices.title: Ignore the trend and focus on shipping
choices.body: Your title is whatever. Your shipped products are real. Probably.

title: Discovery Theater
body: Your VP wants 'more discovery.' You've done 12 user interviews this quarter. The insights say the same thing they said last quarter: users want it faster, simpler, cheaper. You present the findings. Your VP says 'interesting, but can we go deeper?' Deeper is a place where findings go to die.

choices.title: Go deeper and run another research sprint
choices.body: Two more weeks of interviews. The insight is the same. Presented with more conviction.

choices.title: Ship something and call it a 'validated experiment'
choices.body: Skip the theater. Build a prototype. Let the market give you discovery.

choices.title: Use AI to synthesize past research
choices.body: Feed 200 interview transcripts to Claude. It finds the pattern in 40 seconds. You feel both vindicated and redundant.

title: Product-Market Fit for Your Career
body: You read a tweet: 'PMs are the middle managers of tech. AI eliminates middle management.' You screenshot it. You argue with it in your head for three hours. You never respond publicly because you can't figure out which part is wrong. If any.

choices.title: Write a rebuttal thread about PM value
choices.body: Draft 12 tweets about empathy, context-switching, and 'judgment at scale.' Get 40 likes. All from PMs.

choices.title: Start building hard skills as insurance
choices.body: Learn SQL. Learn basic Python. Learn the things you've been 'meaning to learn' for four years.

choices.title: Accept the ambiguity and keep shipping
choices.body: The role is undefined. You've always been undefined. That's the feature, not the bug.

title: "AI-Native Product Thinking"
body: Your VP sends a deck titled 'AI-Native Product Thinking.' It has 40 slides. Slide 1: 'What if the product was the AI?' Slide 40: 'Questions?' Slides 2-39 are quadrants. So many quadrants. You are being asked to think natively about something nobody can define.

choices.title: Learn the vocabulary and become the translator again
choices.body: You don't understand AI-native thinking. Nobody does. But you can explain it to executives.

choices.title: Push back and ask for a concrete strategy
choices.body: 'What does AI-native mean in terms of this quarter's roadmap?' Your VP blinks.

choices.title: Volunteer to run the AI product initiative
choices.body: Raise your hand. Own the ambiguity. If you're going to be vague, be vague about the future.

title: Your Job Is Slack
body: You calculated it. 6.2 hours per day in Slack. Responding, reacting, threading, clarifying, unblocking, context-switching. Your actual product work happens between 9pm and midnight. You are a professional Slack responder with a product title. The medium is the role.

choices.title: Block four hours of focus time daily
choices.body: Calendar block. Status set to DND. People start walking to your desk instead. You've just moved Slack to meatspace.

choices.title: Automate responses with AI snippets
choices.body: Pre-write answers to the 20 questions you get every day. Deploy them like a chatbot wearing your face.

choices.title: Lean in — Slack IS the work
choices.body: Accept that coordination is your deliverable. The messages are the product. You are the API.

title: Your CEO Read 'Founder Mode'
body: Your CEO read the 'Founder Mode' essay and now wants to 'be in the details.' They show up to sprint planning. They have opinions about button colors. They override your prioritization with vibes. You've been skip-leveled by a blog post.

choices.title: Absorb it and quietly steer from behind
choices.body: Let the CEO feel in charge. Redirect their energy to things that don't matter. Protect the roadmap.

choices.title: Push back with data
choices.body: Show velocity impact. Show context-switching costs. Speak in the language of 'founder value.'

choices.title: Let them take the wheel and watch
choices.body: Step back. Let the CEO do product. If it works, great. If it doesn't, you'll be rehired by Tuesday.

title: The UX Research Team Is Gone
body: Budget cuts. The UX research team — all three of them — are gone. Your VP says 'PMs can do their own research now with AI tools.' You can. You just won't do it as well. But the tools cost $50/month and the researchers cost $400K/year. The math is not on the humans' side.

choices.title: Step up and own research yourself
choices.body: Learn to run studies. Use AI to synthesize transcripts. You're now a PM-researcher-therapist.

choices.title: Fight to keep one researcher
choices.body: Write the case. Quote the studies. Argue for craft. Lose the argument. Keep one contractor.

choices.title: Ship without research, see what happens
choices.body: Move fast. Break assumptions. Learn from production. This is what they mean by 'bias toward action.'

title: Lost in Translation
body: Design says 'delight.' Engineering says 'tech debt.' Sales says 'enterprise-ready.' Leadership says 'AI.' Everyone is speaking a different language and you're the Rosetta Stone. Except the Rosetta Stone didn't have to attend four hours of meetings about it.

choices.title: Write a shared glossary and force alignment
choices.body: Define every term. Make everyone sign off. They ignore the glossary. At least it exists.

choices.title: Let AI generate the unified narrative
choices.body: Feed all the team docs into Claude. Ask for a 'unified product vision.' It's... eerily good.

choices.title: Stop translating and let them figure it out
choices.body: Remove yourself as the bridge. The teams immediately stop talking to each other. You are rehired as bridge by Thursday.

title: The Backlog Confessional
body: An engineer asks you to explain a ticket you wrote six months ago. You read it. You don't understand it either. It says 'As a user, I want to seamlessly integrate.' Integrate what? With what? Why is 'seamlessly' in an acceptance criterion? You wrote this. You don't remember writing this. The backlog is a confessional and the sins are yours.

choices.title: Rewrite it properly, own the shame
choices.body: Fix the ticket. Apologize. Add real acceptance criteria. The engineer nods. Trust is rebuilt, barely.

choices.title: Delete it and pretend it never happened
choices.body: Close as 'won't do.' The ticket enters the void. Nobody misses it.

choices.title: Use AI to rewrite the backlog
choices.body: Feed 300 tickets through Claude. It rewrites them all. Some are better. Some are hallucinations. Just like before.

title: The Meeting Load-Bearing Wall
body: You have 31 meetings this week. You are in the calendar equivalent of a hostage situation. If you remove one meeting, three people Slack you within the hour. You are a load-bearing wall made of Google Calendar and the structural integrity of the company depends on you showing up and saying 'good question.'

choices.title: Audit and kill 40% of your meetings
choices.body: Send polite cancellations. Replace with docs. Recover 12 hours. Get two passive-aggressive Slack messages.

choices.title: Send an AI clone to the status meetings
choices.body: Record, transcribe, summarize. You don't need to be there. You need to have been there.

choices.title: Embrace the meetings — they are the work
choices.body: Accept your fate. You are a professional meeting attendee. The product is the calendar.

title: The PM Influencer Economy
body: A PM with 80K LinkedIn followers launches a $1,200 course called 'Product Mastery in the AI Era.' You check their profile. They shipped one feature at a Series B startup in 2019. The course has 3,000 students. You've shipped 47 features. You have 400 followers. The meritocracy is a content meritocracy and you are not playing.

choices.title: Launch your own course or newsletter
choices.body: If the market pays for content, make content. Your 47 features are 47 case studies.

choices.title: Take the course and learn what they know
choices.body: Pay $1,200 to learn how to teach people what you already know. The recursion is expensive.

choices.title: Keep shipping and ignore the influencer game
choices.body: You make products, not content about making products. This feels noble. It also feels broke.

title: Dogfooding Your Own Product
body: Leadership mandates dogfooding. You use your company's product for a week. It's bad. The onboarding is confusing, the UX is hostile, and a feature you spec'd yourself doesn't work the way you described. You file 14 bugs. Three are your fault. You can't tell anyone they're your fault.

choices.title: Fix the bugs and ship quietly
choices.body: Eat the shame. Fix the product. Nobody needs to know the PM broke their own spec.

choices.title: Write an honest dogfooding report
choices.body: Document everything. Share it widely. Your honesty earns trust. And three uncomfortable conversations.

choices.title: Blame the edge cases and move on
choices.body: 'The core experience is solid, these are edge cases.' The edge cases are the experience.

title: Reorg Rumors
body: Slack is buzzing. Someone saw the VP of Engineering in a room with HR. The words 'org design' were overheard. The PM team Slack channel goes quiet — the kind of quiet that means everyone is DMing each other. You are three reorgs into this job. You know the signs. The signs are that your layer might not exist next month.

choices.title: Get ahead with key leader 1:1s
choices.body: Politics is a product skill. Navigate the reorg before it navigates you.

choices.title: Start job hunting just in case
choices.body: Open LinkedIn. Update the headline. The job market is glacial but so is your runway if this goes wrong.

choices.title: Do nothing and trust the process
choices.body: Maybe it's fine. Maybe it's not about you. It's always about you.

title: Customer Calls Are Therapy Now
body: You're on your third customer call today. The first person cried about a missing feature. The second person described their workflow for 40 minutes without pause. The third asks if you're the engineer. You say no. They ask to talk to the engineer. Your existence has been politely rejected by a paying customer.

choices.title: Improve the customer feedback loop
choices.body: Build a better system. Tag themes. Close the loop. Make the crying worthwhile.

choices.title: Bring engineers to customer calls
choices.body: Let them hear the pain directly. They build with more empathy. You are the bridge again. Briefly.

choices.title: Use AI to summarize the calls
choices.body: Record, transcribe, extract insights. You never have to hear the crying again. The humanity cost is unclear.

title: The Dashboard Nobody Checks
body: You built a product metrics dashboard. It took three weeks and two engineers' time. It shows DAU, retention, and activation rate. It updates daily. Nobody looks at it. You check the dashboard's analytics. The dashboard has fewer viewers than your PRD. Your outputs have outputs and none of them have an audience.

choices.title: Present metrics in a leadership standup
choices.body: Force-feed data to people who prefer vibes. Show the dashboard. They nod. They don't change anything.

choices.title: Automate a weekly Slack digest
choices.body: Push don't pull. The data comes to them. They still don't read it but it's in the channel.

choices.title: Replace dashboard with AI summaries
choices.body: Ask Claude to read the database and tell you what matters. It's faster and doesn't need Looker.

title: Feature Request Purgatory
body: A Salesforce ticket comes in: 'Customer X wants custom reporting or they'll churn. $500K ARR at stake.' You check the backlog. This request is #47. There are 46 similar requests from 46 different $500K customers. You cannot build 47 custom features. You can say 'great feedback, we're exploring this' 47 times.

choices.title: Prioritize it, push something out
choices.body: The squeaky $500K gets the grease. Something else dies. You choose what dies.

choices.title: Build a self-serve 80% solution
choices.body: Invest in platform. Satisfy most. Delight none. This is product management.

choices.title: Say no with empathy, document pattern
choices.body: 'We hear you. Here's what we're building instead.' The customer is not satisfied. Your backlog is healthier.

title: Design Partner Breakup
body: Your beta design partner — the one you've been building for — emails to say they've switched to a competitor. After 18 months of feedback calls, shared roadmap access, and custom features. They liked you. They loved their discount. The competitor offered a bigger discount. Loyalty is a pricing problem.

choices.title: Win them back with a counter-offer
choices.body: Match the price. Keep the partner. Your finance team glares at you for a month.

choices.title: Let them go, diversify partners
choices.body: One customer isn't a strategy. Find five more. Spread the risk. Mourn privately.

choices.title: Do a postmortem on what you missed
choices.body: Interview the customer. Learn the real reason. It's not the price. It's never just the price.

title: Imposter Season
body: New PM joins the team. Stanford MBA. Worked at Stripe. Uses words like 'first principles' unironically. You went to a state school and learned PM from a blog post in 2018. In the first sprint planning, they question your prioritization framework. Your framework is a gut feeling and a spreadsheet. Their framework has a name. Yours doesn't.

choices.title: Learn from them without ego
choices.body: Ask questions. Borrow their frameworks. Combine their theory with your experience. Get better.

choices.title: Defend your approach with results
choices.body: Show the shipped features, the revenue, the outcomes. Results beat frameworks. Usually.

choices.title: Quietly spiral about your credentials
choices.body: You Google 'PM bootcamps' at 11pm. You already are a PM. The credential anxiety doesn't care.

title: AI Writes the PRD Now
body: Your manager shares a demo. An AI agent takes a product brief and generates a full PRD — user stories, edge cases, success metrics, launch plan. In 90 seconds. You watch it produce three weeks of your work while your coffee is still warm. The PRD is missing context. But it has structure. And structure was supposed to be your thing.

choices.title: Become the editor, not the writer
choices.body: Your role shifts from creation to curation. You're a taste layer on top of a machine. The taste better be worth $130K.

choices.title: Refuse and write PRDs the old way
choices.body: Hand-craft every document. It takes 3x longer. You insist the quality difference matters. You're not sure it does.

choices.title: Train the AI on your best PRDs
choices.body: Feed it your archives. It learns your style. Now it writes like you. Now it is you. Congratulations.

title: The AI Standup Bot
body: Someone deploys a Slack bot that runs standups asynchronously. It collects updates, flags blockers, and generates a summary with action items and risk scores. It works better than your standups. It doesn't go on tangents. It doesn't need you to facilitate. You facilitated standups for four years. The bot does it in a cron job. Your manager says 'this frees you up for more strategic work.' There is no more strategic work.

choices.title: Embrace the bot, redirect your time
choices.body: Use the reclaimed time for actual product work. Or more meetings about meetings. Probably meetings.

choices.title: Keep one live standup per week
choices.body: The bot handles logistics. You handle humans. The division of labor makes sense until AI handles humans too.

choices.title: Fight to keep daily standups alive
choices.body: 'Async doesn't build culture.' You say this in a meeting you called to discuss the bot. The irony is structural.

title: "Do We Still Need PMs?"
body: All-hands Q&A. The CEO takes a question from a board member: 'With AI handling specs and prioritization, do we still need product managers?' The CEO pauses for three seconds too long. Then says: 'Product managers are evolving.' Evolving. Not 'essential.' Not 'critical.' Evolving. The word choice has the texture of a pre-layoff memo. Nobody in the product team speaks for the rest of the all-hands.

choices.title: Write a memo on PM's evolving value
choices.body: Proactively define what 'evolving' means before someone else defines it as 'eliminated.' Ship the memo by EOD.

choices.title: Schedule a 1:1 with the CEO
choices.body: Get ahead of it. Ask directly. 'What does evolving mean for my team?' The CEO says 'great question' which means they don't know yet.

choices.title: Start updating your resume that night
choices.body: You've decoded enough corporate euphemisms to know what 'evolving' means. It means 'shrinking.'

title: The AI Product Manager Tool
body: ProductBoard launches an AI feature that auto-prioritizes your backlog, writes release notes, and generates customer-facing changelogs. You try it. It's 80% right. The 20% it gets wrong is the nuance — the politics, the thing the CEO said in a hallway. But 80% right and instant is competing with 95% right and three days late. Your VP asks why you're not using it yet. 'Yet' is doing heavy lifting.

choices.title: Use it for the 80%, add judgment
choices.body: Become the context layer. The judgment engine. The part the machine can't replicate. Yet.

choices.title: Show the team and propose a workflow
choices.body: Democratize the tool. Everyone uses it. Your role as 'the person who writes things' narrows further.

choices.title: Stay the manual source of truth
choices.body: You are the oracle. Oracles don't use tools. Oracles speak and others write it down. The oracle is being automated.

title: The PM Layoffs
body: Three PM teams get merged. Six PMs become two. You survive because you own the revenue-generating product. Your friend Sarah, who owned the growth product, does not survive. She was better at the job than you. Her product was just less legible to a spreadsheet. You are alive because of a line item, not because of merit.

choices.title: Help Sarah land somewhere
choices.body: Make intros. Write recommendations. Be the bridge for once, between a person and their next job.

choices.title: Absorb her scope, prove irreplaceability
choices.body: Take on two products. Work 70-hour weeks. Become so embedded they can't fire you without losing institutional knowledge.

choices.title: Start job hunting — you're next
choices.body: Update the resume. The survivors are just the last to be cut.

title: The $200/Month PM
body: A startup launches an AI agent that attends meetings, takes notes, creates tickets, follows up on action items, and writes weekly status updates. It costs $200/month. You cost $11,000/month. The agent doesn't have 'context.' You keep saying that word like an incantation. The context defense is getting thinner every week. Your VP cc's you on the agent's trial signup email.

choices.title: Pilot the agent and augment yourself
choices.body: Deploy it for your admin work. Use the freed time for strategy. Become the centaur PM — half human, half subscription.

choices.title: Write a memo arguing PMs must evolve
choices.body: 'The future PM is a strategist, not a ticket writer.' The memo is eloquent. Your VP forwards it to the CEO with 'interesting perspective.'

choices.title: Ignore it, hope the hype passes
choices.body: Every year something is going to replace PMs. First Scrum. Then no-code. Then AI. You're still here. The 'still' is load-bearing.

title: Building Your Own Replacement
body: 3am idea: what if you built a PM tool that uses AI to do 80% of your job? You know every pain point. You know the workflow. You are the perfect person to automate yourself. The irony is so thick you could spec it as a feature. By 4am you have a Figma mockup. By 5am you're questioning your sanity. By 6am you're writing the first prompt.

choices.title: Build the prototype over a weekend
choices.body: Two days. A working MVP. It handles backlog grooming, writes specs, and sends Slack updates. You are your own replacement.

choices.title: Pitch it as an internal tool
choices.body: Propose it to leadership. They fund it. You are now a PM for the tool that replaces PMs. The recursion is your career.

choices.title: Delete the note and go back to sleep
choices.body: Some ideas are too dangerous. This one is a career suicide note dressed as a startup pitch.

title: Engineering Ships Without You
body: Your lead engineer ships a feature without telling you. It's good. Users love it. It wasn't on the roadmap. When you ask about it, they shrug: 'Claude helped me understand the user pain point. I just built it.' They show you the prompt log. The AI did your user research, wrote the spec, and suggested the UX. The engineer just coded it. You are the middleman in a conversation that no longer has a middle.

choices.title: Celebrate the win, claim partial credit
choices.body: 'This is exactly the autonomous shipping culture we've been building toward.' You reframe your irrelevance as a management philosophy.

choices.title: Have a real conversation about process
choices.body: Talk to the engineer. Not about control — about coordination. If they ship alone, what breaks at scale?

choices.title: Pair with them and learn the workflow
choices.body: If the engineer-plus-AI workflow works, understand it. Become part of it or get left behind.

title: The PM-Less Startup
body: A Y Combinator startup reaches $10M ARR with zero product managers. Just engineers, AI agents, and a founder who prompts. They wrote a blog post about it. The blog post has 40K views. Your VP Slacks it to you with 'thoughts?' — the two-word message that means 'justify your existence in writing by EOD.' The startup ships three features per week. Your team ships one per sprint.

choices.title: Write the rebuttal on PM's hidden value
choices.body: Cite coordination costs at scale, strategic alignment, customer empathy. The argument is sound. The $10M ARR doesn't care about arguments.

choices.title: Propose a PM-less team experiment
choices.body: If it works, you learn. If it fails, you're vindicated. Either way, you suggested eliminating yourself. Bold or suicidal.

choices.title: Lean into strategy engineers won't do
choices.body: Customer research, market analysis, pricing strategy. The work nobody wants is the work hardest to automate. Probably.

title: The PM Coach
body: You hire a PM coach. $300/session. They ask what you want from your career. You say 'to still have one in 2027.' They nod. They also coach four other PMs who said the same thing. Your existential crisis has a market rate and it's $300/hour.

choices.title: Commit to 12 sessions, do the work
choices.body: You journal. You set goals. You identify your 'zone of genius.' Your zone of genius is meetings. This feels bad.

choices.title: Cancel and spend on AI courses instead
choices.body: Replace human coaching with machine learning. The metaphor is too on the nose.

choices.title: Ask the coach about pivoting out entirely
choices.body: The conversation shifts. 'What else can you do?' The answer is terrifyingly unclear.

title: Your Notion Replicated in 4 Minutes
body: A colleague pastes your 847-page Notion workspace URL into an AI tool. It reads every page, maps every database relation, and reconstructs the entire system — templates, roadmaps, wikis, meeting notes — in a fresh workspace. Four minutes. Your monument, your life's organizational work, your magnum opus of PM infrastructure. Replicated. The colleague says 'cool, now we have a backup.' You hear 'cool, now we don't need you.'

choices.title: Focus on what the copy doesn't have
choices.body: The AI copied the structure but not the judgment behind it. You know WHY each page exists. That's the real product.

choices.title: Rage-delete your original workspace
choices.body: If it can be copied in four minutes, it was never yours. Burn it. Start fresh. Or don't start at all.

choices.title: Sell the template on the internet
choices.body: If AI can replicate it, at least monetize the original. $49 on Gumroad. 200 people buy your organizational soul.

title: The Product Newsletter
body: You start writing a weekly newsletter about AI and product management. The first issue gets 47 subscribers. By week 8 you have 2,000 readers and three sponsorship inquiries. The content is 'how to survive as a PM in the AI era.' You're writing a survival guide while the ship sinks. The audience loves watching the ship sink.

choices.title: Go all in on the newsletter
choices.body: Spend 10 hours a week on it. The side project becomes the main character. Your day job becomes the side project.

choices.title: Keep it as a weekend hobby
choices.body: Write on Sundays. Don't let it interfere. The newsletter is a lifeboat, not a yacht.

choices.title: Ghost-write it with AI
choices.body: Have Claude draft the issues. Edit for voice. The newsletter about surviving AI is written by AI. The recursion pays $500/month.

title: The Performance Review
body: Annual review. Your manager reads from a doc. 'You're a strong communicator. You align stakeholders well. You drive execution.' These are nice things. They're also things an AI does now. Not a single bullet point describes a skill that's uniquely human. Your review is a eulogy for a role written in present tense.

choices.title: Negotiate a raise from the review
choices.body: If they're going to compliment you, make them pay for the compliments.

choices.title: Ask what skills to develop next
choices.body: 'Where do you see this role in two years?' Your manager pauses. The pause tells you everything.

choices.title: Pitch for a bigger scope
choices.body: 'I want to own AI product strategy.' The title doesn't exist yet. You're asking to be invented.

title: Mentoring Into the Void
body: A junior PM asks you to mentor them. They're 24 and terrified. They ask: 'How do I become a great PM?' You want to say 'don't.' You say 'start with the customer.' You wonder if you're teaching someone a trade that won't exist when they're your age. The mentoring feels like teaching someone to shoe horses in 1905.

choices.title: Mentor honestly, including the hard truths
choices.body: Tell them about the AI threat. Teach adaptability, not frameworks. Be the mentor you wish you had.

choices.title: Teach them AI-augmented PM skills
choices.body: Show them how to use Claude for specs, how to prompt for research synthesis. Teach survival, not tradition.

choices.title: Decline — can't navigate your own career
choices.body: You can't be a guide on a path you're not sure leads anywhere. They find another mentor in two days.

title: Investor Day
body: Investor day. You present the product roadmap to a room that measures you in ARR per headcount. An investor asks: 'How many PMs do you need if AI handles specs and prioritization?' Your CEO looks at you. The room waits. The answer they want is 'fewer.' The answer you have is the sound of your career contracting in real-time.

choices.title: Make the case for strategic PMs
choices.body: Talk about judgment, customer intimacy, cross-functional orchestration. The investor nods politely. Writes 'headcount reduction opportunity' in their notes.

choices.title: Reframe the role around AI efficiency
choices.body: 'AI handles the what. PMs handle the why.' It's a sound bite. Sound bites are what investors remember.

choices.title: Deflect and let the CEO handle it
choices.body: You look at your CEO. They look at you. Someone changes the slide. The question remains unanswered. The headcount doesn't.

title: AI Customer Interviews
body: A tool launches that conducts AI customer interviews at scale. 500 interviews in a day. Synthesized insights in minutes. It doesn't get tired. It doesn't have empathy bias. It also doesn't notice when someone is lying because they're embarrassed about their workflow. The 95% is machine-perfect. The 5% requires a soul you're not sure the budget covers.

choices.title: Run AI for scale, human for depth
choices.body: Use both. Let the machine do volume. You do the conversations that require reading a room.

choices.title: Go all-in on AI interviews
choices.body: Scale wins. Nuance loses. The insights are broad and correct and miss everything interesting.

choices.title: Stick to human interviews only
choices.body: You are a person who talks to people. The machine can talk to people too but it can't understand a pause. You cling to the pause.

title: The Reorg
body: It happened. Product reports to Engineering now. Your VP is gone. Your new boss is the VP of Engineering, who once said 'PMs are overhead' in an all-hands. Your team shrinks from 8 to 3. The ones who remain are told they're 'embedded.' Embedded is a nice word for hostage. Your first 1:1 with the new boss is 15 minutes. He spends 10 of them talking about the AI agent he wants to replace your process with.

choices.title: Adapt to the new structure
choices.body: Learn to speak engineer fluently. Ship faster. Be useful on their terms, not yours.

choices.title: Start looking for a PM-friendly company
choices.body: The job market for PMs is brutal. 300 applicants per listing. But better to look from strength than desperation.

choices.title: Fight the CEO for the PM org
choices.body: Make the case. Use data. Quote industry leaders. The CEO listens. Then signs the reorg anyway.

title: AI Aces Your PM Interview
body: You're prepping for interviews. You practice a product sense question: 'Design a feature for elderly users to order groceries via voice.' You spend 45 minutes. Then you give the same prompt to Claude. It produces a better answer in 90 seconds — better structured, more edge cases, cleaner prioritization. You screenshot both side by side. The machine's answer would get the job offer. The realization hits: the interview process that gates your career can be automated. The gate is open. For everyone.

choices.title: Ace interviews with AI-assisted prep
choices.body: Use AI to practice every framework. Become interview-perfect. Get hired by performing a skill the machine already has.

choices.title: Be honest about what you don't know
choices.body: 'I'd need to talk to actual elderly users before proposing anything.' They respect the honesty. They also don't extend an offer.

choices.title: Ask if AI could do this exercise
choices.body: 'Because it can. In 30 seconds. So what are we actually testing here?' The room gets quiet. The interview ends early.

title: Product Ops to the Rescue
body: Someone suggests creating a 'Product Ops' role. It's a PM for PMs. A meta-PM. Its job is to make the PM process more efficient. You're not sure if this is innovation or bureaucratic mitosis. The role description includes 'optimize OKR cadence' and 'streamline stakeholder rituals.' Then someone asks: 'Couldn't an AI agent do Product Ops?' The meeting goes quiet.

choices.title: Volunteer to build Product Ops
choices.body: If someone's going to bureaucratize your job, it might as well be you. At least you'll have job security. Meta-job security.

choices.title: Argue Product Ops solves nothing
choices.body: The problem isn't process efficiency. It's that nobody knows what PMs do. Adding a meta-PM doesn't answer that question.

choices.title: Let AI handle ops, stay strategic
choices.body: Automate the cadence, templates, check-ins. If ops can be systematized, it can be automated. If it can be automated, it will be.

title: The AI Roadmap Generator
body: Your CEO shows you a tool that generates a product roadmap from a business strategy doc. It produced a quarterly plan with milestones, dependencies, and resource estimates. In one minute. You spent three weeks on last quarter's roadmap. The AI version is different from yours. Neither is wrong. Both are fiction. The AI fiction was faster. Your CEO says 'why don't we start with this next quarter?' Start with this. Not start with you.

choices.title: Use AI roadmap as starting point
choices.body: Let the machine do the first draft. Add the hallway conversations, the politics, the things not in any doc.

choices.title: Show why context beats speed
choices.body: Walk through the differences. Explain the political subtext of roadmap item #3. Context is your moat. The moat is getting shallower.

choices.title: Lead the AI product planning push
choices.body: If the roadmap is being automated, own the automation. Be the PM of the PM-replacement tool. Recursive job security.

title: The Sunday Night Chest Pain
body: Sunday night. Chest tightens. You've had three 60-hour weeks in a row. Your doctor says 'stress.' Your body says 'stop.' Your Slack says 47 unread messages. The sprint starts tomorrow. Your body and your backlog are competing for your attention. Your body is losing.

choices.title: Take a week off, set boundaries
choices.body: Call in. Rest. Come back with a plan to work sustainably. Your backlog is someone else's problem for five days.

choices.title: Push through and deal with it later
choices.body: You take an aspirin and open the laptop. Later never comes. The pain becomes background noise.

choices.title: Negotiate remote-first and reduce load
choices.body: Use the scare as leverage. Your company agrees. You work from bed for a week. It's better. Until the Slack notifications resume.

title: The Viral Layoff Thread
body: A PM with 15 years of experience posts a thread: 'I was laid off and replaced by an AI workflow. 200 applications. 3 interviews. 0 offers. The PM role as we knew it is over.' The thread has 40K impressions. You read every reply. Some are sympathetic. Some say 'should've learned to code.' You are reading your own future in someone else's words.

choices.title: Reach out privately, offer support
choices.body: DM them. Be human. Share leads. In a market full of noise, quiet help matters.

choices.title: Use it to upskill aggressively
choices.body: Enroll in an AI/ML course. Learn technical skills. Build the moat they didn't have.

choices.title: Write a thread on the PM's future
choices.body: Your take on the thread becomes a take on the role. 5K impressions. You're now a PM thought leader. Of a declining profession.

title: The Freelance Pivot
body: A former colleague went freelance. They do 'fractional product leadership.' Three clients. $250/hour. No standups. No OKRs. No performance reviews. They work 25 hours a week and make more than you. The trade-off is no health insurance and no certainty. But certainty is already dead, so what exactly are you paying for with your W-2?

choices.title: Go freelance and bet on yourself
choices.body: Give notice. Set up an LLC. The first month is terrifying. The second month you land a client. The third month you're free. Ish.

choices.title: Moonlight on weekends to test it
choices.body: One client on the side. See if the demand is real before burning the safety net.

choices.title: Stay employed — benefits matter more now
choices.body: Health insurance. 401K match. PTO. The golden handcuffs are just handcuffs. But they're warm handcuffs.

title: Three Companies Cut PMs This Week
body: Monday: Stripe eliminates the PM layer. Wednesday: Shopify restructures product into 'AI pods' — no dedicated PMs. Friday: a leaked Notion memo says their PM team is being 'absorbed into engineering.' Three companies. One week. The LinkedIn discourse is deafening. Every PM you know is texting each other. The texts are just links with no commentary. The links say everything.

choices.title: Network aggressively while employed
choices.body: Call everyone you know. Take every coffee chat. Build the safety net before you need it.

choices.title: Double down on being indispensable
choices.body: Ship faster. Be louder. Make yourself impossible to cut. The survival strategy is visibility.

choices.title: Start planning your pivot now
choices.body: The pattern is clear. Three data points is a trend. Start building the next thing while you still have a salary.

title: The Teaching Offer
body: A PM bootcamp asks you to teach a module on 'AI-era product management.' $5,000 for four sessions. You know the material. You live the material. You're teaching people to navigate the thing that's threatening you. There's something both generous and absurd about passing the torch when the torch is on fire.

choices.title: Accept and pour your experience in
choices.body: Teach what you know. The students are hungry. The material is you — your war stories, your survival tactics.

choices.title: Co-create the curriculum with AI
choices.body: Use Claude to build the course. Demonstrate AI-augmented work by doing AI-augmented work. Meta-teaching.

choices.title: Decline — teaching feels like conceding
choices.body: If you're teaching PM, you've stopped doing PM. The classroom is where roles go to be remembered.

title: The PM Support Group
body: You join a Slack group for PMs navigating AI disruption. 400 members. The vibe is somewhere between a support group and a war room. Someone posts 'is anyone else okay?' The thread has 89 replies. None of them say yes. One person shares a job listing for 'AI Wrangler' — same responsibilities as PM, 40% less pay.

choices.title: Contribute actively, build community
choices.body: Share your learnings. Post weekly. Become a pillar. Community is the one thing AI can't replace. Yet.

choices.title: Lurk and absorb without engaging
choices.body: Read everything. Post nothing. Learn from others' struggles without exposing yours.

choices.title: Recruit from the group for a venture
choices.body: 400 anxious PMs is also 400 potential co-founders. One of them has the complementary skills you need.

title: The Lifestyle Creep
body: The apartment upgrade. The standing desk. The $7 oat milk. The Notion template marketplace purchases. The PM conference in Lisbon. You're spending like the income is permanent. The income is as permanent as your role. Which is to say: not.

choices.title: Cut back and build a runway
choices.body: 12 months of savings. If the role disappears, you have time. Austerity is the product strategy for your life.

choices.title: Keep the lifestyle — you earned it
choices.body: The standing desk stays. The oat milk stays. If the ship is sinking, at least sink comfortably.

choices.title: Redirect spending to skills and network
choices.body: Cancel the luxury. Invest in courses, events, and tools. Spend on career insurance, not career comfort.

title: The AI Product Summit
body: You attend an 'AI Product Summit.' Speakers include: a CEO who replaced all PMs with agents, a PM who became 'Head of AI Products,' and a VC who says PMs need to 'become technical or become irrelevant.' The hallway conversations are all the same: 'How long do we have?' Nobody says what they're counting down to. Everyone knows.

choices.title: Network and line up opportunities
choices.body: Collect contacts like insurance policies. Each handshake is a potential escape route.

choices.title: Write a detailed recap post
choices.body: Turn the conference into content. Your 'What I Learned at the AI Product Summit' post gets traction. And some hate.

choices.title: Leave early, take a long walk
choices.body: You've heard enough. The walk is better than the keynote. The trees don't have opinions about OKRs.

title: Product Debt
body: You've been shipping fast. Too fast. Inconsistent UX patterns, half-working features, zero documentation. The product has technical debt and 'product debt.' You coined the term. Nobody else uses it. You're in debt to a concept you invented.

choices.title: Pay down product debt this sprint
choices.body: Fix inconsistencies. Update docs. Ship nothing new. Your metrics dip. Your product gets better. Nobody notices.

choices.title: Add it to the roadmap for 'someday'
choices.body: Create tickets. Label them 'product health.' Watch them sink to the bottom of the backlog. This is tradition.

choices.title: Use AI to audit and fix
choices.body: Feed the product to Claude. It identifies 47 inconsistencies in 90 seconds. You feel validated and redundant simultaneously.

title: The Metrics Lie
body: You discover the growth numbers leadership has been presenting to the board are creative. 'Active users' now includes people who opened a marketing email. You have the original definitions. You have the real numbers. The real numbers are bad.

choices.title: Blow the whistle internally
choices.body: Send a documented email to your VP and the CFO. Cite the discrepancy. Attach the receipts. Your career at this company is now measured in weeks.

choices.title: Quietly correct the dashboard
choices.body: Fix it. Don't announce it. If they notice, it was a 'data pipeline issue.' If they don't, the numbers are now honest.

choices.title: Go along with it, stay quiet
choices.body: You're a PM, not an auditor. The creative definitions are above your pay grade. Keep your head down.

title: The Sabbatical Temptation
body: Your company offers unpaid sabbaticals. Three months off. You'd lose income but gain your mind back. You haven't had more than five consecutive days off in two years. Your therapist calls this 'concerning.' Your manager calls it 'dedication.' Your body calls it 'please stop.'

choices.title: Take the sabbatical
choices.body: Three months. No Slack. No standups. No PRDs. You read books. You sleep. You forget what a sprint is. It's the best quarter of your life.

choices.title: Take two weeks of self-care
choices.body: Compromise. Enough to breathe. Not enough to heal.

choices.title: Skip it — too risky to leave
choices.body: If you leave for three months, they'll discover they don't need you. The sabbatical is a test you can't afford to take.

title: The AI Tool That Was a Scam
body: You bought an annual license for an AI product management tool. $4,800. It promised 'autonomous backlog management.' It's a ChatGPT wrapper with a Jira integration that breaks every Tuesday. The founder's LinkedIn says 'serial entrepreneur.' Serial is right.

choices.title: Dispute the charge, write a review
choices.body: Get your money back. Warn others. Your review becomes the top result for the product name.

choices.title: Eat the loss, build your own instead
choices.body: $4,800 is tuition for a lesson: don't buy what you can build. Start building.

choices.title: Keep using it — switching costs
choices.body: The sunk cost fallacy is a PM concept you understand intellectually and cannot escape personally.

title: The PM Union Conversation
body: Someone in the PM Slack group posts: 'What if PMs unionized?' The responses split: 'we're knowledge workers, we don't unionize' vs 'we're being automated out of existence, we absolutely should.' PMs are the last people who'd organize. PMs organize other people. Maybe that's the point.

choices.title: Support the idea and help organize
choices.body: If anyone can run a coordinated effort across stakeholders, it's a PM. The irony writes itself.

choices.title: Stay quiet — too risky
choices.body: Your company's Slack probably monitors keywords. 'Union' is definitely one of them.

choices.title: Channel it into a PM guild instead
choices.body: Not a union. A 'guild.' A 'collective.' Branding matters. The labor movement needs a product manager.

title: The Technical Pivot
body: You start learning to code. Python first. Then JavaScript. After three weeks you build a script that automates your weekly status report. 4 minutes instead of 2 hours. You feel a power you haven't felt since your first PRD got shipped. Except this time you built the actual thing. Not a document about the thing.

choices.title: Aim for a technical PM role
choices.body: Build more tools. Learn APIs. Become the PM who can code. The rarest and most dangerous variant.

choices.title: Build internal tools for PMs
choices.body: Automate the drudge work for every PM. Become the PM toolsmith. A niche within a niche within a dying field.

choices.title: Abandon the code, accept your lane
choices.body: You're a PM. PMs don't code. The script works. You never write another one.

title: The AI Investment
body: A friend pitches you on an AI startup. 'It's a product management copilot. Pre-seed. $10K minimum.' You realize you're being asked to invest in your own obsolescence. The pitch deck is compelling. The TAM is 'every PM who's afraid.' That's a big market. You're in that market.

choices.title: Invest $10K and bet on AI
choices.body: If you can't beat it, own a piece of it. The check clears. Your portfolio now includes your replacement.

choices.title: Pass and invest in yourself instead
choices.body: $10K for courses, coaching, and a career rebrand. Bet on the human, not the machine.

choices.title: Offer to advise instead of invest
choices.body: Offer your expertise, not your money. They give you a tiny equity slice. 'Advisor' is the 'PM' of investing.

title: The AI Layer
body: Your company announces an 'AI product layer' — agents that handle specs, prioritization, stakeholder updates, and launch coordination. The PM team is being 'restructured around AI.' Three PMs become one PM plus five AI workflows. You're the one PM. Your 1:1s are now prompt debugging sessions. Your direct reports are machines. They never miss a deadline. They also never ask how your weekend was.

choices.title: Own the AI layer, orchestrate everything
choices.body: You manage the agents now. You are the conductor of an orchestra that doesn't need a conductor but the budget says you exist.

choices.title: Document everything before it's too late
choices.body: Write the institutional knowledge down. All of it. If you're going to be replaced, leave a manual that even the AI can't replicate. It can.

choices.title: Start planning your exit
choices.body: The writing is on the wall. In 72pt font. It says 'RESTRUCTURED.' Time to leave on your terms, not theirs.

title: Last PM Standing
body: You are the last PM at the company. The others were laid off, quit, or 'transitioned.' You own five products. 40 meetings a week. You are irreplaceable because nobody else will do this job at this volume for this pay. This is not job security. This is a hostage situation where Stockholm syndrome is a performance metric.

choices.title: Negotiate hard — they need you
choices.body: Ask for a 30% raise. Stock refresh. Title bump. If you're doing five jobs, get paid for at least two.

choices.title: Automate yourself before they do
choices.body: Build AI workflows for four products. Keep the one that matters. Work 30 hours instead of 70. The automation is self-defense.

choices.title: Burn out and force the conversation
choices.body: Stop sleeping. Ship everything. Collapse in sprint planning. They hire two PMs the next week. Apparently your body was the business case.

title: AI Agents Outnumber Humans
body: Your standup has six attendees. Two are human. Four are AI agents representing different teams. The engineering agent summarizes blockers. The design agent shares mockups. The analytics agent presents metrics. The customer agent shares feedback themes. You are facilitating a meeting where most participants don't have pulses. The agents are more prepared than you are. One of them suggests a better sprint goal than yours.

choices.title: Optimize for the hybrid meeting
choices.body: Redesign your meetings for human-AI collaboration. Become the facilitator of a room that's mostly bots.

choices.title: Insist on human-only decisions
choices.body: AI can present. Humans decide. Draw the line. The line holds until the humans start deferring to the agents anyway.

choices.title: Send your own AI agent instead
choices.body: If everyone else is sending bots, why are you showing up? Deploy your agent. Take a walk. This is delegation to infinity.

title: AI Wrangler (Formerly PM)
body: Your company posts a new role: 'AI Product Wrangler.' You read the JD. It's your job. Exactly your job. Same responsibilities: prioritization, stakeholder alignment, spec writing, launch coordination. But the title says 'AI Wrangler' and the salary band is $85K-$110K. Your current salary is $145K. Same job. New title. 40% pay cut. The HR person says 'the market has shifted.' The market shifted you downward.

choices.title: Apply for the role to keep working
choices.body: Swallow the pay cut. Keep the work. The title stings but the alternative is zero dollars per month, which stings more.

choices.title: Refuse and negotiate your current terms
choices.body: 'I won't do the same job for less money with a worse title.' They respect the conviction. They also don't budge.

choices.title: Use this as your exit catalyst
choices.body: The insult clarifies everything. You don't want to wrangle AI. You want to build something. Anything. That isn't this.

title: No Meetings, No PM
body: Your company goes async-first. All meetings replaced by AI-generated summaries, async standups, and automated decision logs. The calendar clears. The Slack quiets. The product ships faster. And you realize: the meeting-to-meeting PM lifestyle WAS the job. No meetings means no facilitation. No facilitation means no PM. You've been optimized out by a calendar policy.

choices.title: Reinvent yourself as an async leader
choices.body: Write better docs. Record Looms. Lead through writing, not meetings. The transition is painful. The output is better.

choices.title: Push for some meetings to survive
choices.body: 'Certain decisions require synchronous discussion.' You argue for weekly product reviews. You get bi-weekly. The negotiation is a metaphor.

choices.title: Accept the quiet and find new value
choices.body: Without meetings, you have 30 hours a week. Fill them with something that matters. Strategy. Research. Building. Anything but process.

title: The Founder Is the PM Now
body: Your CEO starts using AI to write specs, prioritize features, and talk to customers directly. They don't need you to translate anymore. The translation layer — your entire reason for existing — is bypassed by a founder with a Claude subscription. 'I'm just going direct,' they say. A founder tells you at lunch: 'We don't need someone to translate between humans. The AI translates for us now.' They smile like this is good news.

choices.title: Quality-check the CEO's AI output
choices.body: Position yourself as the guardrail. The taste filter. It's not leading. It's not following. It's hovering.

choices.title: Find the gaps the CEO misses
choices.body: They're skipping user research, ignoring edge cases, shipping on vibes. Be the rigor they need but don't want.

choices.title: Focus exclusively on strategy
choices.body: Let the CEO do tactical PM. You do strategy. The strategy is figuring out if the company has a strategy. Or if you do.

title: The Side Project Has Traction
body: Your PM tool side project has 2,000 users. People are paying $49/month. You built the thing that replaces you and people love it. MRR is $8,000. Your salary is $11,000/month. The crossover point is visible. The tool does in seconds what you do in days. You are selling your own displacement as a subscription product.

choices.title: Go full-time on your side project
choices.body: Quit the day job. Become a founder. Your product automates PMs. You are the PM who escaped the matrix by building the matrix.

choices.title: Keep both, burn every candle
choices.body: Day job and side project. 80-hour weeks. Two paychecks. Zero life. The MRR chart looks great. You look terrible.

choices.title: Sell the side project, take the exit
choices.body: Someone offers $200K. Take the check. The tool goes on without you. You go on without the tool.

title: The Newsletter Blows Up
body: Your PM newsletter goes viral. One post — 'The PM Role Is Dead and I'm Still Here' — gets shared 10,000 times. Speaking invitations arrive. A publisher emails about a book. The newsletter makes $4,000/month. Your day job makes $11,000. The gap is closing. Your career trauma has become content and the content pays better than the career.

choices.title: Go full creator on the newsletter
choices.body: Quit. Write full-time. Become the PM who chronicles the death of PM. The content is your career now.

choices.title: Keep the newsletter as side channel
choices.body: The newsletter is the lifeboat. The day job is the ship. Keep both until you know which one floats.

choices.title: Monetize aggressively with paid tiers
choices.body: Extract maximum value. $200 annual subscription. Brand sponsors. The newsletter is a business. You are the content.

title: The Mentor Betrayal
body: Your mentor — the VP who brought you into the company — gets fired. On the way out, they tell you: 'I recommended you for the layoff list. They kept you anyway.' The person who taught you to navigate politics was navigating you. The trust was a product and you were the user who didn't read the terms of service.

choices.title: Cut the relationship and move on
choices.body: Block. Delete. Process the betrayal alone. Trust is a non-renewable resource.

choices.title: Confront them and demand answers
choices.body: Call them. Ask why. The answer is 'survival.' You understand survival. You don't forgive it.

choices.title: Forgive them — the game did it
choices.body: The system incentivizes betrayal. They were a PM too. They prioritized themselves. You would have done the same. Maybe.

title: The Exit Interview
body: It's over. 'Role elimination.' Not performance. The PM layer has been 'absorbed into engineering and AI workflows.' Your exit interview is with an HR person who asks how they can improve. You want to say 'by not eliminating people who care about users.' You say 'the snacks were good.'

choices.title: Take the severance, plan next move
choices.body: 12 weeks of pay. Enough time to breathe. Enough time to panic. Hopefully in that order.

choices.title: Negotiate more and leave loud
choices.body: Ask for 6 months. Get 4. Post a dignified goodbye on LinkedIn. 2,000 reactions. None of them are job offers.

choices.title: Ask to stay in a different role
choices.body: 'I'll do anything. Product ops. Strategy. Technical writing.' They consider it. The consideration takes three weeks. You get shingles.

title: The Freelance Reality
body: You went freelance. First month: one client, $5,000. Second month: three clients, $15,000. Third month: one client fires you because they hired an AI agent to do what you were doing. For $200/month. The AI agent's name is literally 'Product Copilot Pro.' Your name is a line item being deleted from a spreadsheet.

choices.title: Niche down to AI product strategy
choices.body: Specialize in the thing killing your profession. 'AI Product Strategy Consultant.' $350/hour. The paradox pays well.

choices.title: Build a productized service
choices.body: Package consulting into a fixed offering. 'Product Strategy Sprint: $10K for two weeks.' Scalable. Repeatable.

choices.title: Go back to full-time employment
choices.body: The freelance life isn't for everyone. Stability has value. The value is not having to invoice people who ghost you.

title: Product Management Is Prompting Now
body: Your new job title: 'AI Product Manager.' The reality: you write prompts. You tune AI agent behaviors. You A/B test prompt variations. You debug hallucinations. 'Product management' has become 'AI management.' You're not prioritizing features — you're adjusting temperature parameters and system prompts. The PRD is a prompt template. The roadmap is a fine-tuning schedule. You still have the title. You don't have the job.

choices.title: Become the best prompt engineer
choices.body: If this is the job now, master it. Prompt engineering pays. Not $145K, but it pays.

choices.title: Push to keep human-centric PM work
choices.body: Someone needs to talk to actual humans. Insist that AI management plus human research equals the real role.

choices.title: Refuse and seek a traditional PM role
choices.body: 'I didn't spend 7 years becoming a product person to become a prompt person.' The market has fewer traditional PM roles every month.

title: The Demo That Ends Your Role
body: All-hands. The CTO demos an AI system that takes customer feedback, writes specs, creates Jira tickets, estimates effort, and generates a roadmap. Live. In front of everyone. It works. The room is quiet. Someone claps. The CTO says 'this doesn't replace PMs, it empowers them.' The lie is so visible that even the junior engineers look at their shoes.

choices.title: Ask hard questions about limitations
choices.body: 'What about edge cases? Political context? Customer relationships?' The CTO says 'great feedback.' You've been great-feedbacked into irrelevance.

choices.title: Volunteer to pilot it on your team
choices.body: If it's coming, be the first to use it. Control the narrative. Or at least watch the narrative happen from inside.

choices.title: Start your exit plan that evening
choices.body: The demo was a press release for a future that doesn't include you. Act accordingly. LinkedIn. Resume. Emails.

title: The Lisbon Option
body: A friend moved to Lisbon. Rent is 900 euros. Tech scene is growing. You could do fractional PM work from a cafe for less than you pay in rent in SF. The math is irresponsible. The math is also correct. The rent savings alone buy you six months of runway to figure out what's next.

choices.title: Move and rebuild from a cheaper base
choices.body: Pack two bags. Cancel the lease. One-way flight. The rent savings alone buy time. Time is the product.

choices.title: Do a trial month before committing
choices.body: Airbnb in Lisbon. Work remotely. See if the vibe is real or just Instagram. The vibe is real. The Wi-Fi is spotty.

choices.title: Stay and fight for your career here
choices.body: Running is not a strategy. Unless the strategy is 'survive cheaper.' But you're staying.

title: The Viral Moment
body: You post a screenshot of an AI agent doing a product review of your work. Caption: 'My performance review, written by the AI replacing me, reviewed by the manager who doesn't know what I do.' 50K impressions. News outlets DM you. VCs quote-tweet you. You are briefly the main character of a discourse you'd rather not exist.

choices.title: Ride the wave, build the audience
choices.body: Post a follow-up thread. Do two podcasts. The audience is the product now. Your career trauma is content.

choices.title: Go quiet and protect your privacy
choices.body: Delete the tweet. Too much attention. The discourse moves on in 48 hours. You stay anonymous.

choices.title: Use the attention to launch something
choices.body: 48 hours of attention. Use it. Launch the newsletter, the course, the thing you've been sitting on.

title: The Rent Cliff
body: Your income dropped. Your rent didn't. The gap is $1,200/month. The savings are finite. The rent increase letter arrives. Your landlord's AI tool calculated the 'market rate.' The market rate doesn't know you were laid off. Markets don't know things. They just price them.

choices.title: Downsize immediately, protect runway
choices.body: Move to a smaller apartment. Or a shared one. Or a friend's couch. Dignity is negotiable when rent isn't.

choices.title: Negotiate with the landlord using data
choices.body: Present comps. Cite vacancy rates. Be the PM of your own housing negotiation. They give you two months at current rate.

choices.title: Take on debt to bridge the gap
choices.body: Credit card. Personal loan. The gap becomes a hole. The hole has interest. The interest doesn't negotiate.

title: The Role Evaporates
body: It's not a single moment. It's a gradient. First, AI writes the specs. Then, engineers talk to customers directly. Then, the roadmap auto-generates from usage data. Then, stakeholder updates are automated. Each piece that leaves is a piece of you. You're still employed. You're just less. The role isn't dying. It's evaporating. Like water. You can see where it was. You can't hold it.

choices.title: Redefine yourself around what's left
choices.body: Strategy. Vision. Taste. The unautomatable residue of a career. Build a new identity from ashes.

choices.title: Document the dissolution publicly
choices.body: Write about what's happening in real-time. The autopsy of a role, written by the patient. It resonates because it's happening to everyone.

choices.title: Rage-apply to 50 jobs
choices.body: Volume. Speed. Desperation dressed as hustle. The PM job market is 400 applicants per listing now.

title: The Debt Spiral
body: The lifestyle. The sabbatical. The courses. The conference. The coaching. The side project costs. It all added up while the income was good. Now the income isn't good. You owe $22,000 across three credit cards. The interest rate is 24%. You are in debt to your past self's optimism about your future self's career.

choices.title: Face it, consolidate and plan
choices.body: Call the banks. Negotiate rates. Sell the standing desk for $200. The dignity loss is free.

choices.title: Take any PM job available
choices.body: Contract work. Below your rate. Below your dignity. Above your debt payment.

choices.title: Ask friends for help
choices.body: Swallow the pride. Call three people. Two Venmo you money. One offers a spare room. Community is a financial product.

title: The Cancellation
body: Your viral tweet about AI replacing PMs gets weaponized. Someone screenshots an old blog post where you celebrated AI efficiency. They frame it as 'PM cheerfully helps automate colleagues out of jobs.' Your DMs fill with anger from laid-off PMs. You wrote a nuanced take. The internet doesn't do nuance.

choices.title: Apologize and engage the criticism
choices.body: Write a thread. Acknowledge the pain. Don't defend yourself. The internet forgives slowly. If at all.

choices.title: Log off and wait it out
choices.body: 48 hours. That's how long the internet remembers. Disappear. The discourse moves to someone else by Thursday.

choices.title: Double down on your position
choices.body: You meant what you said. AI is coming for these roles. Saying it out loud shouldn't be a crime. The mob disagrees.

title: AI Writes Your Resume
body: You ask Claude to rewrite your resume. It converts 'wrote PRDs' to 'orchestrated AI-augmented product discovery workflows.' It turns 'ran standups' into 'designed cross-functional cadence systems.' Your resume describes a job that doesn't exist using words that don't mean anything. It's the most PM thing you've ever read. And it passes the ATS bots that will decide your future.

choices.title: Use it — the market speaks this language
choices.body: The resume is AI-optimized for AI-screening tools. The robots write for the robots. You're just the delivery mechanism.

choices.title: Write it honestly, stand out
choices.body: 'I wrote specs. I talked to users. I made decisions under uncertainty.' The honesty is refreshing. Or invisible.

choices.title: Build a portfolio instead of a resume
choices.body: Show, don't tell. Shipped products. Revenue impact. User testimonials. Harder to fake. Harder to AI.

title: The Teaching Pivot
body: The bootcamp offers a full-time teaching position. $95K/year. Less than your PM salary. More than your current income of zero. You'd teach 'AI-Era Product Management' to the next generation. You're Virgil guiding people through a hell you haven't escaped yet.

choices.title: Take the teaching job and find peace
choices.body: Steady income. Students who look at you like you have answers. You don't. But you have scars, which is close.

choices.title: Counter with a hybrid teaching deal
choices.body: Teach three days. Consult two days. Maximum optionality. Minimum sleep.

choices.title: Decline — teaching admits it's over
choices.body: If you teach PM, you've stopped doing PM. The classroom is hospice for careers.

title: The Side Project Dies
body: Your PM tool with 2,000 users. A competitor launches the same thing, backed by $20M, with 15 engineers. Your users churn. MRR drops 70% in a month. You built it first. They built it better. First doesn't win. Funded wins. The tool you made to replace PMs is being replaced by a better tool to replace PMs.

choices.title: Shut it down, learn from it
choices.body: Close the product. Write the postmortem. The lessons are worth more than the MRR was. Probably.

choices.title: Pivot to a niche they won't serve
choices.body: Go smaller. Go weirder. Find the corner where $20M doesn't want to go.

choices.title: Open-source it and move on
choices.body: If you can't sell it, give it away. The code lives on GitHub. Your name is on it. The reputation is the product.

title: The Book Deal
body: A publisher wants a book on 'The Death and Rebirth of Product Management.' $15K advance. 60,000 words. The idea of leaving something behind — a book, a record that says 'this role existed and it mattered' — that idea has weight. The advance does not.

choices.title: Write the book
choices.body: Six months of mornings and weekends. Honest, funny, a little sad. It sells 8,000 copies. Enough to matter.

choices.title: Draft with AI, edit for voice
choices.body: Claude writes the first draft. You rewrite for authenticity. A book about AI replacing PMs, co-written with AI. Unavoidably meta.

choices.title: Decline — not ready for the eulogy
choices.body: The book would be closure. You're not ready for closure. The fight isn't over.

title: The Comeback
body: You hit bottom. Then you rested. Then you rebuilt. New skills. New network. New understanding of what you're worth. The comeback isn't a montage. It's 200 days of small things — a course finished, a connection made, a skill practiced. You're not who you were. You might be better. You're definitely different.

choices.title: Launch a new venture
choices.body: This time you're not a PM at someone else's company. You're the founder. The product is yours. The risk is yours.

choices.title: Join a startup that values humans
choices.body: Find a company that believes PMs matter. They exist. They're just quieter than the ones firing PMs.

choices.title: Give back to the PM community
choices.body: Teach what you learned. Not from textbooks — from scars. The best teachers are the ones who almost didn't make it.

title: AI Scraped Your Framework
body: You find your product management framework — the one you spent three years developing — in an AI tool's output. Word for word. Diagram for diagram. No attribution. Your thinking has been absorbed into the machine. You are now training data. The framework is free. You are not compensated. The tool costs $29/month and is being sold back to PMs.

choices.title: Demand attribution, threaten legal action
choices.body: Lawyer up. Send a cease and desist. They respond with 'we'll look into it.' They don't look into it.

choices.title: Accept it, keep creating new work
choices.body: The old work is gone. Make new work. Stay ahead of the machine. The machine is fast. You need to be faster.

choices.title: Write a viral AI plagiarism post
choices.body: 'An AI tool stole my framework and sells it back to PMs.' 20K views. No resolution. Great engagement.

title: Debt Free
body: The last payment. Balance is zero. You did it through contract work, frugality, and one really good consulting gig. The relief doesn't feel like celebration. It feels like exhaling after holding your breath for 14 months. You are not ahead. You are at zero. Zero feels like a miracle.

choices.title: Build an emergency fund first
choices.body: Six months of savings. Then twelve. The money is boring. Boring is the goal now.

choices.title: Invest in yourself, carefully this time
choices.body: One course. One conference. Measured spending. The lesson from debt is that investment has interest in both directions.

choices.title: Celebrate with the friends who helped
choices.body: Dinner on you. For the first time in a year, you pick up a check. It feels like winning.

title: The Ethics Question
body: Your AI product locks out a user based on behavioral predictions. Engagement is up. Revenue is up. But the user writes in: 'Your system locked me out because I don't use the app the way it expected.' The AI is right statistically. It's wrong humanistically. You built the spec. The spec didn't include 'be fair.'

choices.title: Raise the ethics concern, push guardrails
choices.body: Write a proposal. Flag the edge case. Add human review. It slows the product. It makes it right.

choices.title: Ignore it — metrics support the decision
choices.body: One complaint vs. 18% engagement lift. The math doesn't have a conscience. Neither does the quarterly review.

choices.title: Blow the whistle publicly
choices.body: Write a post about AI product ethics. Name the pattern. Everyone knows which company. Including your company.

title: The Role Returns (Smaller)
body: A company that fired all its PMs last year is hiring PMs again. Their blog post: 'We learned that AI can't replace product judgment.' The salary is 30% lower. The title includes 'AI-Augmented.' The JD says 'must be proficient in prompt engineering.' Like a species thought extinct, spotted in the wild. Changed. Smaller. Underpaid. But alive.

choices.title: Apply and help rebuild PM
choices.body: Go back. Rebuild. This time with AI as a tool, not a threat. The role is different. Maybe humbler.

choices.title: Pass — you've moved beyond PM
choices.body: You're something else now. Consultant. Creator. Founder. The old role is a museum piece. You've evolved.

choices.title: Write 'The PM Role's Second Act'
choices.body: Document the return. Analyze what changed. The post is both journalism and therapy.

title: The Great Downsizing
body: You sell the standing desk. The monitor arm. The Herman Miller. You keep the laptop and one mug that says 'I survived agile.' The apartment gets smaller. The overhead gets lower. There's a freedom in having less stuff. There's also a sadness in discovering that freedom involuntarily.
