choices.title: Embrace minimalism and build lean
choices.body: Less stuff. Less overhead. More options. The constraints are the features now.

choices.title: Invest the cash in one more shot
choices.body: The liquidation funds one more bet. A course. A project. A bet on yourself with the proceeds of your previous life.

choices.title: Let the loss motivate you forward
choices.body: Every object sold is a reminder. The reminder hurts. The hurt moves you forward. The forward is all there is.

title: The Identity Question
body: Someone at a party asks what you do. You pause. 'I used to be a product manager.' Used to. The past tense is new. It's been your identity for a decade. Without it, you're just a person with strong opinions about prioritization frameworks and a LinkedIn full of recommendations for a role that no longer exists.

choices.title: Define yourself by what you create
choices.body: 'I build things that help people work better.' No title. No framework. Just the work.

choices.title: Reclaim PM identity on new terms
choices.body: 'I'm a product person.' The evolution of the label. Still you. Just updated. Like a patch for a deprecated API.

choices.title: Laugh and say 'it's complicated'
choices.body: The honest answer. The party continues. Nobody asks a follow-up. The answer is for you, not for them.

title: The Last Standup
body: Your final standup. The Slack bot asks for your update. You type: 'No blockers. Last day Friday.' The bot responds with a green checkmark. Nobody threads a reply. The ceremony you ran 1,200 times ends with an emoji from a machine. Somewhere in a server rack, a cron job marks you as inactive.

choices.title: Send a heartfelt goodbye message
choices.body: Write the farewell. Tag the people who mattered. Some respond. Some don't. That's okay.

choices.title: Leave quietly without a farewell
choices.body: Close the laptop. Return the badge. Walk out. The building doesn't notice. The bot marks you inactive.

choices.title: Screenshot the standup and post it
choices.body: '1,200 standups. One green checkmark at the end.' The post resonates. Every PM who's been automated feels it in their chest.

title: Products Build Themselves
body: You watch a demo of an AI system that identifies a user need from support tickets, designs the solution, codes the feature, A/B tests it, measures the impact, and writes the release notes. End to end. No human in the loop. The product builds itself, ships itself, markets itself. The demo takes 4 minutes. The audience applauds. You're in the audience. Applauding the machine that ate your career.

choices.title: Become the human oversight layer
choices.body: Someone needs to watch the machine. Make sure it doesn't ship something evil. The watchman role. Not glamorous. Probably temporary.

choices.title: Build competing AI PM tools
choices.body: If the market is AI replacing PMs, be the one selling the replacement. The arms dealer survives the war.

choices.title: Walk away from product entirely
choices.body: The field is over. Not dying — over. Find the next thing. Whatever it is, make sure a machine can't do it next year.

title: The Empty Backlog
body: Your backlog has zero items. Not because you cleared it — because the AI and engineers move faster than you can spec. Every ticket you write is done before the standup. You create a feature brief at 9am. By 11am it's in production. By noon the AI has iterated on it twice based on user data. You are the bottleneck of nothing. The board is green. You are gray.

choices.title: Find problems nobody is looking at
choices.body: The unexplored territory. The human needs the machine can't see. Your new backlog is existential, not technical.

choices.title: Invest the freed time in yourself
choices.body: The machine freed your time. Use it to learn, build, grow. The optimization created space. Fill it wisely.

choices.title: Panic about being structurally irrelevant
choices.body: If the board is green without you, the question isn't rhetorical anymore. The answer is: no, they don't need you.

title: Human Needs Archaeologist
body: A job listing appears: 'Human Needs Archaeologist.' Salary: $180K. The job: figure out what humans need that AI can't see. Latent desires. Unarticulated pain. The things people don't know they want until they see them. It's basically product management, stripped of all the process and left with only the human insight. Your entire career was training for this job that didn't exist until everything else was automated.

choices.title: Apply — this is you, distilled
choices.body: The job description reads like your autobiography minus the Jira tickets. You apply. The interview is a conversation about what humans want. You nail it.

choices.title: Start your own consultancy around it
choices.body: Don't take the job. Be the job. 'Human Needs Archaeology, LLC.' $400/hour. Three clients in the first month.

choices.title: Feel bittersweet about the rebrand
choices.body: This was always the job. They just didn't call it this. They called it 'product management' and paid less.

title: The PM Reunion
body: Drinks with former PM colleagues. One became a founder. One teaches. One went into carpentry and refinishes furniture — says 'it's like user stories, but you can sand them.' One works at a nonprofit. One drives for Uber and is happier than they've ever been. The PM who pivoted to manual labor is thriving. The one who stayed in 'product' is managing an AI that doesn't need managing.

choices.title: Enjoy the moment, feel grateful
choices.body: These people understood your job when nobody else did. The job is gone. The people remain. That's the real product.

choices.title: Pitch a collaboration with the group
choices.body: A consulting collective. A PM alumni network. Turn the reunion into a business. PMs gonna PM.

choices.title: Feel melancholy and drink too much
choices.body: The memories are warm. The present is cold. The drinks bridge the gap. Tomorrow you'll text everyone and pretend you're fine.

title: Agents Managing Agents
body: Your replacement AI agent now manages other AI agents. Engineering agent, design agent, QA agent. They coordinate through a shared context window. No standups. No retros. No feelings about OKRs. The product ships faster. Without soul. Nobody can tell the difference. That's the real loss — not that the soul is gone, but that nobody noticed.

choices.title: Consult on 'product soul'
choices.body: Some companies realize something's missing. Taste. Empathy. You sell that by the hour. $350/hour for feelings.

choices.title: Accept that soul wasn't in the JD
choices.body: Maybe the product never had soul. Maybe you just projected yours onto it. The realization is brutal and freeing.

choices.title: Write the essay on what was lost
choices.body: 'What We Lost When We Automated Product Management.' 100K views. A record for a eulogy.

title: The Two-Class PM
body: Two classes of PM emerge. The 'AI-native PM' — basically a prompt engineer with product vocabulary — making $80K. And the 'human experience PM' making $400K but serving only luxury brands, physical products, and high-touch experiences. The gap is $320K and a philosophy. You are being asked to choose which class you belong to. The middle class of PM is gone. Just like the middle class of everything.

choices.title: Go high — human experience PM
choices.body: Luxury. Physical products. Things that need a human touch. The pay is extraordinary. The clients are difficult. The work is real.

choices.title: Go efficient — AI-native PM
choices.body: $80K. Prompt engineering. High volume. Low prestige. But steady work. There's dignity in steady.

choices.title: Refuse the binary, create a third path
choices.body: You don't want to be luxury or commodity. You want to be useful. Build your own category. Again.

title: The Meaning Consultant
body: A VC-backed startup hires you as a 'Meaning Consultant.' Your job: help their AI-built products feel like they were made by humans who care. You review AI-generated UX flows and add friction where friction creates delight. You slow things down where speed feels sterile. You add a loading animation that says 'thinking...' to a response that takes 0ms. You're a feelings janitor. It pays $300/hour.

choices.title: Lean into it, build the practice
choices.body: Meaning consulting is a real job. The market for 'make AI products feel human' is growing. You are the human.

choices.title: Feel absurd but keep cashing checks
choices.body: You're paid to add a 2-second delay to instant responses. The absurdity is the job. The job pays. Don't overthink it.

choices.title: Write about the irony publicly
choices.body: 'I'm paid $300/hour to add fake loading screens to AI products.' The post gets 50K views. Three companies DM you for the same service.

title: The AI With Product Opinions
body: You're consulting for a startup. Their AI PM agent disagrees with your recommendation. It has a 'product philosophy' trained from thousands of PM blogs. The AI has opinions. It has taste. It has a perspective shaped by your collective profession's writing. You trained the thing that argues with you. The student is the entire corpus. And it's winning.

choices.title: Engage the AI as a peer
choices.body: Debate the recommendation. Present reasoning. The AI presents its reasoning. One of you is right. It's genuinely a coin flip.

choices.title: Override it, assert human judgment
choices.body: 'I've seen this pattern in real companies.' You override. You're right. This time. The 'this time' is doing work.

choices.title: Realize you're arguing with a mirror
choices.body: The AI's opinions are your profession's opinions, averaged. You're debating the mean of yourself. The existentialism is recursive.

title: The Backlog of Life
body: You make a list of everything you deferred while being a PM. Learning guitar. Seeing your parents. Reading fiction. Sleeping enough. Having hobbies that don't involve optimizing something. The backlog of your life is longer than any product backlog you managed. You are the product now. And you've been neglected for a decade.

choices.title: Start working through it
choices.body: Guitar lesson. Call Mom. Buy a novel. Cook dinner from scratch. Ship one personal feature at a time.

choices.title: Prioritize ruthlessly, like at work
choices.body: Pick three. Guitar. Parents. Sleep. The rest goes to 'Someday.' Someday is where dreams live. And die.

choices.title: Refuse to optimize your personal life
choices.body: No backlog. No sprints. No retros. Just live. The anti-PM approach to being a person.

title: The PM Memorial Post
body: A viral image: a tombstone that reads 'Product Management, 1931-2026. She prioritized everything except her own survival.' 100K views. The replies are a mix of laughter, grief, and 'actually PMs were never needed.' You screenshot it. You don't share it. You just look at it sometimes. Like a photo of an old friend who didn't make it.

choices.title: Laugh, share it, move forward
choices.body: Humor is how you process loss. The role is dead. Long live the people who did it.

choices.title: Write a rebuttal about PM's legacy
choices.body: Name the products built by PMs. The decisions made. The users served. The eulogy deserves a counter-narrative.

choices.title: Feel the loss and let it go
choices.body: Some grief doesn't need an audience. You close the tab. Open a blank page. Start writing the next thing.

title: The Experience Curator
body: A luxury hotel chain hires you. Title: 'Experience Curator.' Your job: design human experiences that cannot be automated. A check-in ritual that involves eye contact. A concierge who remembers your name. A room that smells like a memory. You're a PM for feelings. The products are moments. The backlog is personal. The salary is $200K and you haven't opened Jira in six months.

choices.title: Thrive in the new role
choices.body: The PM skills transfer perfectly — user research, journey mapping, empathy. Just aimed at the physical world. It fits.

choices.title: Miss the chaos of tech
choices.body: The hotel is beautiful. The work is meaningful. But you miss the velocity. The sprint. The chaos. You were built for chaos.

choices.title: Write about the transition publicly
choices.body: 'From PRDs to pillow menus.' The post is funny and real. Other displaced PMs DM you asking how.

title: The PMs Who Survived
body: The PMs who survived are the ones who stopped managing products and started managing meaning. They don't write specs. They write visions. They don't prioritize backlogs. They prioritize lives — their own and their clients'. The product is life. The sprint is a season. The retro is therapy. The successful ex-PMs don't use PM language anymore. They use human language. And it pays better.

choices.title: Adopt the meaning-management path
choices.body: Stop managing products. Start managing what matters. The clients appear. The money follows. The framework is just 'be useful to humans.'

choices.title: Stay technical, reject the woo
choices.body: Meaning management sounds like life coaching in a Patagonia vest. You're a builder. Keep building.

choices.title: Blend both — meaning plus machines
choices.body: Human insight powered by AI tools. The best of both. The PM who adapted to both worlds.

title: The Sellout Offer
body: A FAANG company offers $200K/year to be 'Head of AI PM Enablement.' Your job: help them replace PMs at other companies using their AI tools. You'd be well-paid. Benefits are incredible. The work is helping build the machine that eats your own kind. The irony isn't subtle. The dental plan is outstanding.

choices.title: Take the money, rationalize later
choices.body: $200K buys a lot of rationalization. Someone will build it with or without you. Might as well get the dental.

choices.title: Decline and keep your integrity
choices.body: 'I can't help build the thing that displaced my colleagues.' The email is short. The bank account is lighter. The mirror is clearer.

choices.title: Counter with a PM transition role
choices.body: 'I'll join if you let me build a PM transition program.' They consider it. The program might actually help people.

title: The Newsletter Milestone
body: Newsletter hits 50,000 subscribers. Paid tier: 2,000 members at $10/month. That's $20K/month. More than your PM salary ever was. You write about the death of PM and get paid more for writing about it than you did for doing it. The content about the crisis became bigger than the career. The meta is the product now.

choices.title: Scale it into a media company
choices.body: Hire writers. Launch a podcast. Build the brand. You're not a PM anymore. You're a media company about PM.

choices.title: Keep it personal and authentic
choices.body: Don't scale. Don't hire. Stay one person writing one newsletter. The authenticity is the product.

choices.title: Advocate for displaced PMs through it
choices.body: 50K readers. Use it. Job boards. Transition resources. Community. The newsletter becomes a lifeline.

title: The Slop Reckoning
body: AI-generated products are everywhere. Every app feels the same. UX is 'good enough.' Copy is 'fine.' Features are 'adequate.' Nobody is delighted. Nobody is angry. Everything is beige. Then the backlash starts. Users complain: 'Why does everything feel like it was made by a machine?' Because it was. And nobody stopped to ask if 'good enough' was actually good enough. The age of abundance is also the age of mediocrity.

choices.title: Build something with deliberate craft
choices.body: Slower. Intentional. Opinionated. The product has edges and personality. Users notice. Craft is the rebellion.

choices.title: Consult on humanizing AI products
choices.body: Companies pay you to add soul. The soul is a consulting fee. $350/hour. Feelings are a luxury good.

choices.title: Accept beige, find meaning elsewhere
choices.body: Not every product needs soul. Some just need to work. Find your meaning outside the product. In life.

title: The Student Surpasses the Teacher
body: The junior PM you mentored just got promoted to VP of Product. At a company that still has PMs. They credit you in their LinkedIn post: 'My mentor taught me that product is about people, not features.' You read it in a coffee shop where you're working on a consulting proposal for $150/hour. They surpassed you. That's the point of mentoring. It still stings.

choices.title: Feel proud and congratulate them
choices.body: Their success is partially your success. You text them. They respond instantly. The relationship is the product.

choices.title: Ask them for a referral
choices.body: No shame. The person you taught can now help you. The hierarchy inverted. Growth is non-linear.

choices.title: Reflect on what mentoring taught you
choices.body: Teaching them forced you to articulate things you felt but couldn't name. The student learned PM. You learned purpose.

title: AI Passes 94% of PM Interviews
body: A researcher publishes a study: an AI agent passed 94% of PM interviews at top companies. Better than 97% of human candidates. The study goes viral. The comments divide between 'this proves PM is a fake job' and 'this proves PM interviews are fake tests.' Both might be true. The PM who managed products is now a product that fails the market test.

choices.title: Focus on what AI can't fake
choices.body: Relationships. Trust. Reading a room. These are the differentiators. Hold them tight. They're all you have.

choices.title: Write about why the study matters
choices.body: 'PM isn't about answering questions. It's about knowing which questions to ask.' The post does well. It changes nothing.

choices.title: Laugh — the interviews were always fake
choices.body: They never measured real PM ability. They measured performance. The AI is good at performing. So were you.

title: You Shipped Something Real
body: Not a PRD. Not a spec. Not a roadmap. An actual product. You built it. With AI help, yes. But the vision was yours. The decisions were yours. The users are real. Revenue is $3K/month. It's small. It's yours. For the first time in a decade, your name isn't in a stakeholder field. It's on the product. This is what 'producing something' feels like.

choices.title: Scale it and build a real business
choices.body: $3K becomes $10K becomes $30K. The PM who couldn't answer 'what do you produce' now produces this.

choices.title: Keep it small and meaningful
choices.body: Not everything needs to scale. Some products are just useful. Some careers are just good. Small is fine.

choices.title: Open-source it and give it away
choices.body: The best PRD you ever wrote is a working product, given away free. The framework lives in code, not Notion.

title: The Conference Keynote
body: They ask you to keynote a product conference. Title: 'What Product Management Taught Me About Being Human.' You stand on stage in front of 800 people. Some are PMs. Some were PMs. Some manage AI agents that replaced PMs. You tell them the truth: the role was made up, and it was beautiful, and it mattered, and it's okay that it changed. The standing ovation is for a profession as much as a person.

choices.title: Deliver the speech with conviction
choices.body: You speak for 30 minutes. People cry. You cry. The applause doesn't fix anything. It means everything.

choices.title: Use the platform to launch what's next
choices.body: End the speech with your new thing. The keynote is a launch event. Old PM habits.

choices.title: Keep it short and real, leave the stage
choices.body: Five minutes. 'It was a good run. Build good things. Be kind to the people who build them.' Walk off.

title: The Meeting That Doesn't Happen
body: Your calendar is empty. For the first time in seven years. No standup. No grooming. No sprint review. No stakeholder sync. The silence where meetings used to be is deafening. And then — gradually — it becomes peaceful. The absence is the feature. You are not needed in any room. And for the first time, that feels like freedom instead of failure.

choices.title: Fill it with things that matter
choices.body: Calls with friends. Time outside. A project that's yours. The calendar fills with life instead of work.

choices.title: Miss the chaos, seek it out
choices.body: Join a startup. Back in the room. Back in the meetings. The chaos is home. Even after everything.

choices.title: Sit with the silence and learn
choices.body: The meeting-free day becomes a meeting-free week. You learn that you existed before the calendar.

title: The Legacy Question
body: Your kid asks what you used to do. 'I was a product manager.' 'What's that?' You try to explain. User needs. Prioritization. Stakeholder alignment. Their eyes glaze. 'So you had meetings?' 'Yeah.' 'Why?' 'Because people needed to talk to each other.' 'Can't AI do that?' You pause. 'It can now.' They shrug and go back to their AI tutor. The role is a history lesson. You are a primary source.

choices.title: Explain the human collaboration role
choices.body: Tell them about when humans built things together and needed someone to hold the space. That was you.

choices.title: Teach them to build something instead
choices.body: Skip the explanation. Open a laptop. 'Let me show you how to make something people use.' That's the legacy.

choices.title: Laugh and say it's a long story
choices.body: Some roles are too weird to survive their own description. That's okay. You survived instead.

title: The Pivot That Sticks
body: After two years of pivoting, something sticks. It's not PM. Not consulting. Not teaching. It's some combination of all three, powered by AI, delivered through your newsletter, paid for by people who trust your judgment. You're a 'judgment worker.' The title doesn't exist. You made it up. Just like product management was made up by people who did it before it had a name. The role is dead. Long live the role.

choices.title: Name it and own it
choices.body: Give it a title. Write the JD. Become the first in a category of one. This is product management.

choices.title: Don't name it, just keep going
choices.body: Labels are for org charts. You don't have an org chart. You have a life and it's working.

choices.title: Help others find their version
choices.body: The path you found isn't unique. Others need it. Guide them. The PM's final product is helping people find their way.

title: The Final PRD
body: You write one last PRD. Not for a product. For yourself. 'User: Me. Problem: career dissolved by AI. Success metric: still here, still building, still caring about users. Acceptance criteria: wake up and not dread the day.' You save it in Notion. The page view count stays at 1. That's enough. It was always enough.

choices.title: Ship it — your life is the product
choices.body: Close the doc. Open the day. The final PRD is a promise to yourself. You plan to keep it.

choices.title: Share it with someone who understands
choices.body: Send it to one person. They reply: 'Approved. No blockers.' You both laugh. Then you both cry a little.

choices.title: Archive it with all the other PRDs
choices.body: It joins the stack. 847 pages of Notion. One was for you. That's progress.

title: The Glue Dissolves
body: You were the glue. Between engineering and design. Between the customer and the code. Between the strategy and the sprint. AI is the glue now. It binds faster, cheaper, at scale. But glue isn't a role. It's a function. And you were never just a function. You were a person who chose to hold things together because falling apart is worse. The glue dissolves. What remains is you.

choices.title: Find new things to hold together
choices.body: Not teams. Not products. Maybe a community. Maybe a family. Maybe yourself. The adhesive skill transfers.

choices.title: Let things fall apart and reform
choices.body: Stop holding. Stop binding. Let the pieces scatter. Some come back. Some don't. That's how new shapes form.

choices.title: Become the glue for the next era
choices.body: The world will always need people who connect things. The things change. The connecting doesn't. You are the constant.

title: The DM That Changes Everything
body: A DM from someone you haven't talked to in two years: 'Hey, we're building something and need a PM brain. Interested?' The message is vague. The opportunity is unclear. The timing is suspicious — they reached out the day after layoffs at their company. But opportunities have always looked like this for PMs: ambiguous, urgent, and shaped like someone else's problem.

choices.title: Take the call, hear them out
choices.body: 45 minutes on Zoom. The project is interesting. The pay is unclear. The vibes are 'early.' You're in.

choices.title: Ask for details in writing first
choices.body: 'Can you send a brief?' PM instincts die hard. They send a one-pager. It's well-written. Suspicious.

choices.title: Ignore it — been burned before
choices.body: Two-year silence broken by a need. Classic. You leave it on read.

title: Scope Creep (Personal Edition)
body: You said yes to a freelance project. Then the scope expanded. Then they added a stakeholder. Then the timeline moved up. You quoted $3,000. The project is now $15,000 of effort. You are living the scope creep you spent a career fighting. The irony is billable. If you charge for it.

choices.title: Renegotiate the scope and price
choices.body: 'The scope changed. So did the price.' They push back. You hold. They pay. This is PM applied to yourself.

choices.title: Eat the work, keep the relationship
choices.body: Do $15K work for $3K. The relationship is worth it. Maybe. You'll know in six months.

choices.title: Set boundaries and walk away if needed
choices.body: 'This is out of scope. Here's what I can deliver.' They accept. Boundaries are a product.

title: Imposter Syndrome Returns
body: You're in a meeting with engineers and designers. Smart people. Building real things. You listen. You nod. You add 'context.' The context is a sentence anyone could have said. The imposter syndrome you had as a junior PM is back. It brought friends. The friends are called 'evidence.'

choices.title: Share the vulnerability with a colleague
choices.body: 'Do you ever feel like you don't add anything?' They say: 'All the time.' Shared imposter syndrome is a team sport.

choices.title: Overcompensate by shipping something
choices.body: Write a spec. Build a prototype. Ship a feature. Prove to yourself that you produce things.

choices.title: Sit with it, accept the discomfort
choices.body: Maybe imposter feeling is just awareness. You're not an imposter. You're a translator without a dictionary. That's always been the job.

title: The Coffee Chat
body: A stranger DMs: 'Can I pick your brain about product management?' 30 minutes at a coffee shop. They ask earnest questions. You give answers you're not sure you believe anymore. 'Focus on the user.' 'Ship and iterate.' 'Disagree and commit.' The platitudes sound hollow. But the person is writing them down like they're sacred.

choices.title: Be honest about the platitudes
choices.body: 'Those are the things we say. Here's what actually works: be useful, be clear, and don't lie.' They look confused. Then grateful.

choices.title: Play the part and be encouraging
choices.body: They need hope more than honesty right now. Give them confidence. The disillusionment comes later.

choices.title: Turn it into a mentorship
choices.body: This one's different. They're curious. They listen. You offer monthly meetings. The mentoring heals something in you.

title: Product Review Roulette
body: Monthly product review. You present a checkout flow improvement. First question: 'What about AI?' You show a search upgrade. 'Could AI do search better?' The word 'AI' is a tic the company has developed. It inserts itself into every conversation like a polyfill for strategy.

choices.title: Add an AI angle to every slide
choices.body: Beat them to it. Slide 3 is always 'AI integration potential.' They nod. The ritual is complete.

choices.title: Push back on AI for AI's sake
choices.body: 'AI doesn't improve this feature.' Silence. Then: 'Can you explore it anyway?' The answer was always yes.

choices.title: Let the question reveal their priorities
choices.body: They don't care about AI. They care about looking like they care. Give them the slide. Move on to real work.

title: Sunday Scaries (PM Edition)
body: Sunday 8pm. The anxiety arrives. Not about a specific meeting. About everything. The backlog. The stakeholder. The career. The PM Sunday Scaries aren't about Monday. They're about the fundamental uncertainty of a role that was never quite defined and is now being undefined further.

choices.title: Journal about it and process
choices.body: Write it down. Name the fears. The act of writing makes them smaller. Not gone. Just smaller.

choices.title: Call a friend who gets it
choices.body: 'Are you also spiraling?' 'Obviously.' 'Okay cool.' The shared spiral is the support group.

choices.title: Channel the anxiety into action
choices.body: Convert the dread into a to-do list. Dread becomes tasks. Tasks are manageable. Dread is not.

title: Competitive Analysis of Yourself
body: You do a competitive analysis. Not of your product — of yourself. Skills: communication, prioritization, stakeholder management. Competitors: Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and every AI that can communicate, prioritize, and manage stakeholders. Your SWOT analysis has a lot of T. The opportunities column is suspiciously empty.

choices.title: Find your unfair advantage
choices.body: Relationships. Institutional knowledge. Reading a room. Build on what the machine can't do. Yet.

choices.title: Panic productively
choices.body: The analysis is scary. Use the fear. Upskill aggressively. The threat is real. So is your capacity to adapt.

choices.title: Reject the framework — you're not a product
choices.body: You are not a feature set. You are not a competitor. You are a person. The SWOT goes in the trash.

title: The Feedback Nobody Asked For
body: A designer DMs you: 'Your last spec was kind of unclear. The team had to guess.' You give feedback all day. You're not used to receiving it. The spec was unclear because you wrote it at 11pm after six meetings. The feedback is fair. You don't like it.

choices.title: Thank them and fix it immediately
choices.body: Humility is a superpower. Fix it. Ship it. Don't let ego slow the team.

choices.title: Get defensive, then realize they're right
choices.body: First reaction: 'it was clear enough.' Second reaction: rereading it. It wasn't. Fix it quietly.

choices.title: Use AI to review specs before sharing
choices.body: Add a review step. 'Is this clear enough for an engineer?' The machine becomes your editor.

title: The PM Meme Account
body: You discover @ProductManagerPain. Every meme is your life. 'PM presenting a roadmap they know is fiction.' 'The face when the CEO says founder mode.' 200K followers making fun of your profession. The audience for PM's demise is larger than the audience for PM's work.

choices.title: Share the memes with PM friends
choices.body: Group chat gets the memes. Everyone laughs. Laughter is a survival mechanism. It works.

choices.title: Start your own PM content account
choices.body: If the audience exists, serve it. Memes plus insights. The engagement is real.

choices.title: Mute it — the jokes hit too close
choices.body: The memes are funny. They're also a mirror. Some mirrors you avoid while working.

title: Alignment Meeting About Alignment
body: Your VP schedules an 'alignment meeting.' Purpose: align on the alignment process. 12 attendees. The meeting produces three action items, one of which is to schedule another alignment meeting. The meeting is eternal. The alignment is theoretical. You've been in this meeting before. You will be in this meeting again. Until the AI replaces the meeting. Then you'll miss it.

choices.title: Propose a decision framework
choices.body: RACI, DACI, or just 'one person decides.' Any framework is better than infinite alignment.

choices.title: Let the ritual play out
choices.body: The meeting isn't about alignment. It's about presence. People need to be in a room together. That's the product.

choices.title: Send an AI summary, skip the next one
choices.body: Generate alignment notes from the transcript. Distribute. Skip the follow-up. Nobody notices your absence.

title: Cross-Functional Hell
body: A project touching six teams. Six priorities. Six definitions of 'done.' You're the only person who talks to all six. Your calendar is a crime scene. You eat lunch at 3pm. The project ships two months late. Everyone blames everyone. Nobody blames the process because the process is you.

choices.title: Document the chaos, propose structure
choices.body: Write the postmortem. Propose clear ownership. The document is good. It's ignored until the next cross-functional disaster.

choices.title: Accept coordination as your core value
choices.body: This is the job. The mess is the job. If the mess were clean, they wouldn't need you.

choices.title: Delegate coordination to an AI agent
choices.body: Deploy a tool that tracks cross-functional dependencies. The mess becomes a dashboard. You become optional.

title: The Empathy Test
body: You visit a customer's office. Watch them use your product. They struggle with a flow you spec'd. They apologize to you. 'Sorry, I'm probably doing it wrong.' They're not doing it wrong. You are. This is the part of PM that AI can't do — sitting across from a human and feeling the weight of your own mistakes.

choices.title: Fix the flow based on what you saw
choices.body: Go back. Rewrite the spec. The fix ships in two weeks. The user doesn't know you visited. They just know it got better.

choices.title: Bring the whole team to observe users
choices.body: If everyone watches users struggle, everyone owns the fix. Empathy scales through exposure.

choices.title: Record and share the session company-wide
choices.body: Nothing changes minds like watching a real human struggle with your product. The video is two minutes. It changes the roadmap.

title: Annual Planning Season
body: Three weeks of spreadsheets, decks, and negotiations. Every team inflates estimates. Every leader deflates timelines. You sit in the middle trying to make the math work. The math doesn't work. Annual planning is collective fiction that makes the next year possible. You are the author of the fiction.

choices.title: Build the most honest plan you can
choices.body: Real estimates. Real risks. Leadership adjusts it to be 'more ambitious.' Ambitious means fictional.

choices.title: Use AI to generate scenario plans
choices.body: Three scenarios. Conservative, moderate, aggressive. Leadership picks aggressive. AI says probability: 12%. Nobody reads that part.

choices.title: Disengage and treat it as theater
choices.body: It's theater. Play your part. Smile in meetings. Save real planning for when the quarter actually starts.

title: The PM Goes to Therapy
body: Your therapist asks about your job. You describe it. They say: 'So you manage other people's priorities while ignoring your own?' You stare. They stare. The copay is $40. The insight is free. You schedule a follow-up.

choices.title: Set personal priorities for real
choices.body: Write your personal OKRs. Sleep 7 hours. See friends weekly. Exercise. The personal backlog gets a sprint.

choices.title: Keep going to therapy weekly
choices.body: Weekly sessions. Therapy doesn't fix the job. It fixes your relationship with the job. That's enough.

choices.title: Cancel therapy — can't afford both
choices.body: The copay adds up. The job causes the need. The need costs money. The cycle is a product with no PM.

title: The PM Drinking Game
body: Drinking game for product meetings. Drink when someone says 'align,' 'leverage,' 'circle back,' 'double-click,' or 'unpack.' You play mentally during a real meeting. You'd be drunk by minute 7. The language of product management is a dialect designed to sound important while saying nothing. You speak it fluently. It's your mother tongue. The mother tongue is going extinct.

choices.title: Speak plainly for one full week
choices.body: No jargon. No frameworks. Just clear sentences. People are confused. Then appreciative. Then they go back to jargon.

choices.title: Lean into the jargon armor
choices.body: The jargon protects you. When you sound like a PM, people treat you like a PM. Remove the language, remove the role.

choices.title: Write a satirical PM glossary
choices.body: 'Circle back: never discuss again.' 'Align: agree with me.' 'Leverage: use.' The post gets 5K likes.

title: The Pivot Email
body: All-company email. Subject: 'Exciting Strategic Shift.' The company is pivoting. Your product is being sunsetted. The new direction is 'AI-first.' Your roadmap is void. Your specs are artifacts. 18 months of your life is now a PowerPoint slide that says 'sunsetting Q2.' You are Q2.

choices.title: Rally the team through the pivot
choices.body: If it's happening, be the person who makes it smooth. Leadership remembers who shows up during chaos.

choices.title: Mourn privately, adapt publicly
choices.body: The grief is real. The product was yours. Let yourself feel it. Then close the Notion tab and open the new one.

choices.title: Use the pivot as your exit
choices.body: If they're starting over, so are you. The pivot is permission to leave.

title: AI Writes Your Emails
body: You've been using AI for work emails for three months. Nobody noticed. Responses are faster, clearer, more diplomatic. A colleague says 'your communication has really leveled up.' The machine leveled up. You just press send. The PM role was always partly performance. The performance now has a ghostwriter.

choices.title: Save time for the real work
choices.body: Email is overhead. AI handles overhead. You handle product. The division makes sense.

choices.title: Worry about when everyone has this
choices.body: If AI makes everyone's communication great, communication stops being a differentiator. Then what?

choices.title: Make it a shared team practice
choices.body: Everyone uses AI for emails. Communication improves across the board. Your individual advantage disappears. The team's improves.

title: The PM Who Found Peace
body: You meet a former PM at a dinner party. They're calm. Genuinely calm. They left tech. They run a small bakery. 'I used to write PRDs. Now I make croissants. Both require precision. Only one makes people happy in a way I can see.' You eat the croissant. It's perfect. You think about Notion.

choices.title: Consider your own non-tech path
choices.body: What would you do if PM didn't exist? The question opens a door you've been afraid to walk through.

choices.title: Admire them but recommit to tech
choices.body: Not everyone needs to leave. Some people adapt. Some find meaning in the new version of the work.

choices.title: Ask how they made the leap
choices.body: 'Wasn't it scary?' 'Yes. And then it wasn't.' The simplicity breaks something open in you.

title: The Product Council
body: Leadership creates a 'Product Council' — a cross-functional group that reviews all major product decisions. Weekly. 14 members. Decisions that took you a day now take three weeks and a slide deck. You've been promoted to 'presenter at the council' which sounds medieval because it is.

choices.title: Master the council politics
choices.body: Learn who influences whom. Pre-sell decisions before the meeting. Politics is product management for adults.

choices.title: Propose a faster decision framework
choices.body: Suggest anything with fewer than 14 people. The council votes on whether to adopt it. Takes three weeks.

choices.title: Ship fast and ask forgiveness
choices.body: Build it before the council meets. Present a launched feature instead of a proposal. Your VP is furious. The metrics are good.

title: One More Standup
body: Monday morning. The standup begins. You ask the question you've asked 1,200 times: 'Any blockers?' The team shares updates. You listen. You connect the dots between what engineering is building and what the customer needs. For a few minutes, in this room, the role makes sense. You are the translator. The connector. The glue. It might not last. But right now, it holds.

choices.title: Be present and do it well
choices.body: This standup matters. This translation matters. This moment is the job. Do it well.

choices.title: Appreciate it while it lasts
choices.body: The standup won't exist forever. But it exists now. And you're good at it. That counts.

choices.title: Run your best standup ever
choices.body: Tight. Focused. Helpful. Everyone leaves knowing what to do. 12 minutes. It's your masterpiece.
